network.overall_strategy: The network combines the strongest experimentally supported glycine-forming modules while keeping every encoded step atom-balanced: a surface cyanosulfidic Strecker/aminonitrile branch, a hydrothermal glyoxylate branch fed by either UV dehydration of glyoxylic acid hydrate or Fe2+-mediated isocitrate cleavage, a direct hydrothermal peracetic-acid amination route, and hydrothermal serine thermolysis. To avoid the under-justified shortcut criticized in earlier attempts, the glyoxylate-to-glycine step retains the documented hydroxylamine plus Fe0/Fe2+ chemistry and closes redox bookkeeping explicitly with an iron oxidation product. Ten pathways arise because formaldehyde and ammonia naturally relay between these modules.

reactions.name: Cyanosulfidic Strecker formation of aminoacetonitrile

conditions.other: anoxic HCN-rich evaporitic or tidal-flat pool; concentration during drying and reaction during rewetting

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia first forms an imine/iminium equivalent with formaldehyde, then cyanide adds to give the aminonitrile; the net condensation releases water.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) place aminoacetonitrile in the cyanosulfidic network as the Strecker aminonitrile precursor to glycine. Writing water explicitly corrects the bookkeeping problem noted in earlier failed attempts. The route is experimentally well supported, although aminonitrile stability under intense UV and fluctuating pH remains a recognized limitation (Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of aminoacetonitrile to glycine

conditions.other: wet phase after cyanosulfidic concentration; neutral to mildly alkaline water

reactions.mechanism: The nitrile hydrates stepwise through an amide-stage equivalent and then to the carboxylic acid, releasing ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: This is the direct glycine-forming step from the Patel et al. (2015) cyanosulfidic framework. With inferred stoichiometry the encoded species set corresponds to aminoacetonitrile + 2 H2O -> glycine + NH3, which fixes the under-specified hydrolysis from prior attempts. Side reactions and the persistence of aminoacetonitrile remain open issues, but the step itself is experimentally grounded (Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: UV dehydration of glyoxylic acid hydrate to glyoxylate

conditions.other: UV-irradiated shallow pool under anoxic photoredox conditions

reactions.mechanism: Photochemical loss of water from the gem-diol regenerates the aldehydic glyoxylate form.
reactions.reasoning: Liu et al. (2021) showed UV photoredox access to glyoxylate from 2,2-dihydroxyacetic acid/glyoxylic acid hydrate. Water is written explicitly so the dehydration is balanced. This is a strong surface photochemical entry point into the glyoxylate-glycine network (Liu et al., 2021).

reactions.name: Fe-assisted reductive amination of glyoxylate with hydroxylamine

conditions.catalyst: ferrous iron (Fe2+); Fe0 supplies reducing equivalents
conditions.other: anoxic alkaline hydrothermal fluid or vent mixing zone; ferrous hydroxide used as explicit iron oxidation sink

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxylamine donates nitrogen to glyoxylate through an N-O-containing intermediate, and Fe0/Fe2+ drive reduction to the amino acid.
reactions.reasoning: Muchowska, Varma, and Moran (2019) experimentally demonstrated glycine formation from glyoxylate and hydroxylamine with Fe0/Fe2+ at 70 C. The literature shorthand omits explicit redox products; the balanced net encoded here corresponds to glyoxylate + hydroxylamine + 2 Fe0 + 2 H2O -> glycine + 2 Fe(OH)2, using ferrous hydroxide as a plausible anoxic alkaline sink for oxidized iron. This keeps the experimentally supported hydroxylamine donor and addresses the bookkeeping problem that undermined earlier attempts. Hydroxylamine availability and exact iron mineralogy remain open questions (Muchowska et al., 2019).

reactions.name: Fe2+-catalyzed cleavage of isocitrate to glyoxylate and succinate

conditions.other: anoxic hydrothermal water; metabolic-analog network chemistry

reactions.mechanism: Fe2+ acts as a Lewis acid and promotes retro-aldol cleavage of the C6 tricarboxylate into a C2 glyoxylate fragment and a C4 succinate fragment.
reactions.reasoning: Muchowska et al. (2019) reported Fe2+-promoted cleavage of isocitrate to glyoxylate plus succinate under mild hydrothermal conditions, providing a prebiotic analog of isocitrate lyase. This gives a second experimentally supported entry into the glyoxylate hub without adding artificial connectivity (Muchowska et al., 2019).

reactions.name: Amination of peracetic acid by ammonia to glycine
reactions.mechanism: Ammonia attacks the activated peroxyacetyl carbonyl, and collapse of the peroxide-derived intermediate gives glycine in the net stoichiometry.
reactions.reasoning: Aubrey, Cleaves, and Bada (2008) reported glycine formation from peracetic acid and ammonia under submarine hydrothermal conditions. Including water explicitly gives a balanced net reaction. The major caveat is the uncertain prebiotic supply of peracetic acid itself, which the review identifies as unresolved (Aubrey et al., 2008).

reactions.name: Thermal decomposition of serine to glycine and formaldehyde
reactions.mechanism: Retro-aldol cleavage of the Calpha-Cbeta bond releases the hydroxymethyl side chain as formaldehyde and leaves the glycine backbone.
reactions.reasoning: Bada, Shou, Man, and Schroeder (1978) directly demonstrated serine -> glycine + formaldehyde under hydrothermal heating. Writing formaldehyde explicitly preserves mass balance and reveals a chemically meaningful bridge from hydrothermal amino-acid degradation into the surface aminonitrile module (Bada et al., 1978).

pathways.name: Surface Strecker-hydrolysis route
pathways.description: Formaldehyde, HCN, and ammonia in a cyanosulfidic surface pool form aminoacetonitrile, which hydrolyzes during a wet phase to glycine.

pathways.name: Direct aminonitrile hydrolysis
pathways.description: If aminoacetonitrile is already available, simple aqueous hydrolysis gives glycine directly.

pathways.name: UV glyoxylate-hydrate route
pathways.description: UV dehydration of glyoxylic acid hydrate generates glyoxylate, which is then converted to glycine by Fe-assisted reductive amination.

pathways.name: Direct hydrothermal glyoxylate amination
pathways.description: Glyoxylate present in Fe-rich hydrothermal water is directly converted to glycine with hydroxylamine.

pathways.name: Isocitrate cleavage route
pathways.description: Hydrothermal Fe2+-catalyzed cleavage of isocitrate produces glyoxylate, which then feeds the Fe-assisted amination step to glycine.

pathways.name: Peracetic acid amination route
pathways.description: Peracetic acid reacts with ammonia under hydrothermal conditions to give glycine directly.

pathways.name: Serine thermolysis route
pathways.description: Hydrothermal retro-aldol decomposition of serine yields glycine and formaldehyde.

pathways.name: Serine-to-aminonitrile relay
pathways.description: Serine thermolysis liberates formaldehyde; after transport into a cyanosulfidic surface pool it can be trapped as aminoacetonitrile and hydrolyzed to an additional glycine equivalent.

pathways.name: Strecker-peracid tandem route
pathways.description: Surface Strecker chemistry yields aminoacetonitrile and then glycine; the ammonia released on hydrolysis can be recaptured by hydrothermal peracetic acid to generate a second glycine equivalent.

pathways.name: Serine-driven multi-module glycine amplification
pathways.description: A hydrothermal-surface-hydrothermal relay: serine decomposition supplies formaldehyde for Strecker aminonitrile formation, and the hydrolysis-released ammonia is then reused in peracetic acid amination, giving three glycine equivalents overall.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Strong literature-backed Strecker/hydrolysis sequence. rxn_001 is chemically reasonable for surface Strecker/cyanosulfidic chemistry, and rxn_002 is the standard aminonitrile hydrolysis to glycine. The main correction is stoichiometry: rxn_002 should be encoded as aminoacetonitrile + 2 H2O -> glycine + NH3. Surface aqueous conditions are otherwise appropriate.
suggestions: Encode rxn_002 with 2 H2O explicitly.
If rxn_001 is meant to track Patel et al. closely, specify the aqueous cyanosulfidic or wet-dry context.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Very solid single-step conversion from the key intermediate aminoacetonitrile to glycine. The only concrete correction is that rxn_002 should be written as aminoacetonitrile + 2 H2O -> glycine + NH3. Otherwise this is well aligned with the Patel et al. aminonitrile hydrolysis chemistry.
suggestions: Add the missing 2 H2O coefficient in rxn_002.
State the aqueous hydrolysis conditions more explicitly.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Both component reactions are literature-backed, but the pathway bridges surface UV chemistry to hydrothermal Fe-driven amination without an explicit transport or concentration step for glyoxylate. rxn_004 is only balanceable when written as glyoxylic acid + hydroxylamine + 2 Fe + 2 H2O -> glycine + 2 Fe(OH)2, and that Fe(OH)2 bookkeeping should be justified because the cited work treats Fe0 and Fe2+ as promoting agents rather than isolated stoichiometric products.
suggestions: Add an explicit transport or concentration justification for glyoxylate between the surface and hydrothermal settings.
Encode rxn_004 with 2 Fe and 2 H2O and clarify whether Fe(OH)2 is intended as net redox bookkeeping or an observed product.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Direct target formation from glyoxylate is chemically plausible and literature-supported. The main issues are stoichiometric specification of rxn_004 and the fact that the encoded Fe(OH)2 sink is a plausible redox closure rather than the exact literature representation of Fe0 and Fe2+ promoted reductive amination. rxn_004 should be written as glyoxylic acid + hydroxylamine + 2 Fe + 2 H2O -> glycine + 2 Fe(OH)2 if that is the intended net transformation.
suggestions: Encode rxn_004 with 2 Fe and 2 H2O explicitly.
Clarify whether Fe(OH)2 is a bookkeeping product and note the hydrothermal Fe0 or Fe2+ conditions and hydroxylamine source.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Coherent hydrothermal sequence from isocitrate to glyoxylate to glycine, strongly aligned with Muchowska et al. The main limitation is still rxn_004: it needs 2 Fe and 2 H2O explicitly, and the conversion of iron to Fe(OH)2 is a plausible bookkeeping choice but not the exact literature formulation of the Fe0 and Fe2+ promoted chemistry.
suggestions: Keep the Fe2+ catalytic condition explicit for rxn_005.
Correct rxn_004 stoichiometry and explain the iron oxidation product.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Direct, balanced hydrothermal route with literature support from Aubrey et al. The encoded chemistry is acceptable as written. The main residual uncertainty is upstream availability of peracetic acid, which the literature identifies as an open question rather than a flaw in this particular step.
suggestions: Add the experimental temperature or pH window for rxn_006 if available.
If this route is central to the network, justify how peracetic acid is generated or replenished upstream.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Strongest single-step module in the network. rxn_007 is balanced, mechanistically sensible as serine retro-aldol cleavage, and directly supported by hydrothermal decomposition studies. The assigned hydrothermal environment is appropriate.
suggestions: State the hydrothermal temperature regime or residence time from the cited experiments.
If serine is intended as a network entry point, indicate its upstream source or concentration mechanism.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Each reaction is individually plausible, but the combined relay is weaker than the underlying modules. It assumes formaldehyde from hydrothermal rxn_007 survives transport and capture into the surface Strecker chemistry of rxn_001 before competing reactions, and rxn_002 still needs 2 H2O. Because rxn_007 already produces glycine, this is better framed as an amplification motif than a minimal route.
suggestions: Add an explicit transport or capture step for formaldehyde between the hydrothermal and surface environments.
Correct rxn_002 to include 2 H2O.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Chemically reasonable tandem use of the Strecker module and the peracetic acid module, with NH3 effectively recycled from rxn_002 into rxn_006. The cascade is not directly demonstrated, and the surface-to-hydrothermal handoff of the NH3-bearing inventory should be stated explicitly. rxn_002 also needs 2 H2O.
suggestions: Describe how the NH3 inventory is retained or transferred between the surface and hydrothermal modules.
Correct rxn_002 to include 2 H2O.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the most speculative composite pathway. All individual reactions are plausible, but the full sequence requires a hydrothermal-to-surface formaldehyde relay followed by a surface-to-hydrothermal ammonia relay, neither of which is explicitly justified in the encoded network. It therefore reads more like a possible network coupling than a demonstrated route. rxn_002 needs 2 H2O.
suggestions: Add explicit transport or concentration steps for both formaldehyde and NH3 across environments.
Correct rxn_002 to include 2 H2O and distinguish this amplification motif from a minimal linear pathway.

evaluation.network_feedback: Connected network with sufficient size and no isolated subgraphs. The deterministic balance check reports no conservation-violating reactions, but two reactions are only balanceable with omitted coefficients and should be corrected explicitly: rxn_002 should be aminoacetonitrile + 2 H2O -> glycine + NH3, and rxn_004 should be glyoxylic acid + hydroxylamine + 2 Fe + 2 H2O -> glycine + 2 Fe(OH)2 if ferrous hydroxide is the intended redox sink. Core modules are well aligned with the literature and the network clearly reaches glycine by multiple chemically credible routes. The main remaining weaknesses are the non-literal literature representation of rxn_004, the lack of explicit transport or concentration justification for cross-environment relay pathways, and unaddressed literature challenges around hydroxylamine supply and peracetic acid generation. mol_010 would also be clearer if annotated explicitly as Fe(OH)2. Overall this is a good network, but it remains just below the 0.9 approval threshold until stoichiometry and environmental handoffs are made more explicit.
